lesson.title: Picking a Direction: One-Sided vs Two-Sided Tests
lesson.summary: A one-sided test uses a directional alternative hypothesis, greater than or less than, concentrating the evidence check in a single tail of the sampling distribution, while a two-sided test's not-equal alternative splits the check across both tails.
lesson.body:
The alternative hypothesis, as the previous chapter showed, can take three forms: p greater than some value, p less than some value, or p not equal to some value. The first two are called one-sided, or one-tailed, alternatives, because they claim the parameter has moved in one specific direction. The third is called two-sided, or two-tailed, because it only claims the parameter is different, without committing to a direction, so evidence in either direction counts.

This choice has a direct, calculable effect on the p-value. In a one-sided test, the p-value is the probability, assuming H0 is true, of getting a test statistic at least as extreme as the one observed, in the specific direction named by Ha, only one tail of the sampling distribution is in play. In a two-sided test, 'as extreme' means as far from the null value in either direction, so both tails contribute, and for a symmetric distribution like the normal curve, the two-sided p-value works out to roughly double the one-sided p-value for the same observed test statistic.

Worked numeric illustration: suppose a hypothesis test produces a z test statistic of 2.05. Using the standard normal distribution, the area beyond z = 2.05 in a single tail is about 0.0202, roughly 2 percent. If the alternative hypothesis were one-sided in the matching direction, such as Ha: p greater than the null value, the p-value for this test is that single tail area, about 0.0202. If instead the alternative hypothesis were two-sided, Ha: p not equal to the null value, the p-value must also count the mirror-image tail below z = negative 2.05, doubling the area to about 0.0404. The same data and the same test statistic can therefore produce noticeably different p-values, and potentially a different decision at a fixed significance level such as 0.05, depending purely on how the alternative hypothesis was framed.

That sensitivity is exactly why the direction of Ha has to be decided before looking at the data, based on a genuine prior research question, such as the cereal-box example from the previous chapter, where the consumer group specifically suspected the true proportion was lower than advertised, justifying a one-sided Ha: p less than 0.20. Choosing a direction only after seeing which way the data leaned, in order to make a result look more significant, defeats the purpose of the test and inflates the chance of a false positive. Used honestly, a one-sided test is simply the more precise tool for a question that already has a specific direction built into it, while a two-sided test is the appropriate default whenever the research question is genuinely open to change in either direction.
